newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK Bank ready to act vs mid-price home speculation.
newsitem.headline: HK Bank ready to act vs mid-price home speculation.

text.p: Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp Ltd said on Friday it was prepared to reconsider its mortgage criteria if it saw a speculative bubble building in Hong Kong's medium price residential property market.
But the HSBC Holdings Plc unit's general manager, Christopher Langley, stressed Hongkong Bank did not now see any sign of a bubble.

Langley told a media briefing he thought the small number of banks active in the luxury end of the market, which has surged in a speculative run, were already reconsidering their lending policies, adding Hongkong Bank was not a player in that segment.
"My own view is that this particular speculative run is just about to come to an end anyway," Langley said.

"I think there are now too many players in the market who understand that the level of price increases that we've seen over the last six months simply are not sustainable for very much longer, and therefore you start to get a situation where the downside risk is much much heavier than the upside possibility of profit," he said.
Langley said the encouraging aspect about the recent run-up in luxury residential prices was the lack of spillover into the medium price residential market.

"If our bank does see any clear indications of a significant speculative bubble starting in the medium price residential property market, then we will certainly be prepared to relook at our retail mortgage parameters, but at the moment we do not see any sign of that," he said.
Langley said recent comments by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), the territory's de facto central bank, had been extremely helpful in trying to depressurise the speculative surge.
He declined to say whether Hongkong Bank had held any discussions with the HKMA on the matter.

The HKMA said earlier this week that banks needed to exercise additional care in relation to their property exposure in the current environment, and should look critically at their lending criteria, particularly for more expensive properties.

Raymond Li, acting deputy chief executive of the HKMA, said earlier this week that while institutions should adhere strictly to the 70 percent loan-to-value ratio, a lower ratio would normally be appropriate for more expensive properties.
